source_refs.note: Topic 23.3.1 (PDF 104-106); the mechanisms, the DNPH equation and Figure 23.2 are redrawn. The Perspex intermediate is named 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile (the caption says '2-ethyl'); '2,4-NDPH' is read as 2,4-DNPH.

blocks.text: Aldehydes and ketones react with hydrogen cyanide to form cyanohydrins (hydroxynitriles). HCN itself is not used directly because it is an extremely poisonous gas; instead it is made in the mixture by slowly adding a mineral acid (HCl) to an aqueous solution of sodium or potassium cyanide and the carbonyl compound.

blocks.alt: Ethanal (H3C and H on a C double-bonded to O; C +delta, O -delta) + H-CN (H +delta, CN -delta), KCN/HCl over the arrow, gives 2-hydroxypropanenitrile: a C carrying H3C, OH, H and CN.
blocks.caption: Ethanal and HCN give 2-hydroxypropanenitrile (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 104).

items: CH3COCH3 + HCN -> (CH3)2C(OH)CN (2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile), KCN/HCl; it is an intermediate in making the polymer Perspex.

blocks.alt: Propanone (two H3C groups on a C double-bonded to O; C +delta, O -delta) + H-CN, KCN/HCl over the arrow, gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile: a C carrying two H3C groups, OH and CN.
blocks.caption: Propanone and HCN give 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 105).

blocks.text: Mechanism: HCN is neither a good nucleophile nor a strong enough acid to give many cyanide ions, so a slight excess of KCN is used, leaving some free CN- ions that start the reaction and keep it going at a reasonable rate.

items: CN- attacks the delta+ carbonyl carbon and the C=O pi electrons move onto oxygen, giving an anion: RCHO + CN- <=> RCH(O-)CN.
The anion takes a proton from HCN, giving the hydroxynitrile and regenerating CN-: RCH(O-)CN + HCN <=> RCH(OH)CN + CN-.

blocks.alt: Three steps. i) KCN (Excess) + HCl (Limiting) -> HCN (Nucleophilic Reagent) + KCl. ii) RHC=O (C +delta, O -delta) + cyanide ion, :C-triple bond-N with a negative charge, in equilibrium with the anion R, H, O- and C-triple bond-N on one carbon. iii) That anion + H-CN (H +delta, CN -delta) in equilibrium with the hydroxyalkanenitrile (OH in place of O-) + cyanide ion.
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the addition of HCN (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 105).

blocks.text: Nitriles can be hydrolysed by dilute acid or aqueous alkali to carboxylic acids or carboxylate ions (topic 23.4.1).

Since aldehydes and ketones are made by oxidising alcohols, alcohols can be made by reducing them. With a reducing agent such as NaBH4 or LiAlH4, aldehydes give primary alcohols and ketones give secondary alcohols: CH3CHO + 2[H] -> CH3CH2OH (NaBH4, water/OH-); CH3COCH3 + 2[H] -> CH3CH(OH)CH3, propan-2-ol (NaBH4, alkaline aqueous solution). The [H] in brackets stands for hydrogen supplied by the NaBH4 to balance the equation; it does not mean atomic hydrogen.

blocks.alt: Two equations. Ethanal, CH3-C(=O)-H, + 2[H], with NaBH4 and delta (heat) over the arrow and H2O/OH- under it, gives ethanol, CH3-CH2-OH. Propanone, CH3-C(=O)-CH3, + 2[H], with NaBH4 Heat over the arrow and alkaline aqueous solution under it, gives propan-2-ol, CH3-CH(OH)-CH3.
blocks.caption: Reduction of ethanal and propanone with NaBH4 (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 105).

blocks.alt: The hydride ion H:- (nucleophile) attacks the carbon of RHC=O (C +delta, O -delta; carbonyl compound): one curly arrow goes from the hydride's lone pair to C, another from the C=O bond to O. This gives the alkoxide ion R-CH2-O-. With H-OH (H +delta, OH -delta) over the next arrow, it gives the alcohol R-CH2-OH + :OH-.
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the reduction of a carbonyl compound by a hydride ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 106).

blocks.text: Aldehydes and ketones undergo a condensation reaction with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) to give orange crystalline solids with well-defined melting points. The reagent adds across the C=O group and a molecule of water is then eliminated. For example, ethanal gives orange crystals of ethanal 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone: CH3CHO + H2N-NH-C6H3(NO2)2 -> CH3CH=N-NH-C6H3(NO2)2 + H2O.

blocks.alt: Ethanal (H3C and H on C=O) + H2N-NH- attached to a benzene ring with NO2 opposite and O2N next to it (2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine) -> ethanal-2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone, in which the C=O has become C=N-NH- on the same ring, + H2O. Drawn as two rows: reactants, then products.
blocks.caption: Ethanal and 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine give ethanal-2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone and water (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 106).

blocks.text: This reagent is used to identify carbonyl compounds. Carboxylic acids, esters, acyl halides and amides, which also contain a C=O group, do not give this test.

blocks.alt: Two test tubes: one of yellow-orange liquid, and one packed with orange crystals.
blocks.caption: Figure 23.2: Ethanal gives orange crystalline 2,4-DNPH (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 23.2).
